ann_34.text: This part acts on 89 of 242 training patients (37%), and 53 of them had heart disease.
Through it, age lowers the predicted risk only once it rises above about 59 years: going from 29 to 68 years moves a typical patient from about 20% to about 14% (on the training data only).
Over 42 to 66 years, it lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 15% (on the training data only).

For the typical patient it acts on (a 64-year-old man with 1 vessel coloured, a flat ST segment, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy and resting blood pressure of 140 mm Hg), it changes the predicted risk only slightly, which stays at about 99% (on the training data only).

ann_35.text: This part acts on 154 of 242 training patients (64%), and 63 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old man with resting blood pressure of 140 mm Hg, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG and 0.5 mm of ST depression), it lowers the predicted risk from about 37% to about 24% (on the training data only).

Through it, higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 13%, and an ST segment that does not slope up raises it from about 20% to about 28% (on the training data only).
For patients with an upsloping ST segment, resting blood pressure lowers the predicted risk here only once it rises above about 111 mm Hg, and only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_36.text: This part acts on 42 of 242 training patients (17%), all of them patients with atypical angina; 8 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 52-year-old man with atypical angina, no ST depression and a maximum heart rate of 164 beats per minute), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 2% to about 5% (on the training data only).
Through it, atypical angina rather than any other chest pain type raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 41% (on the training data only).

ann_37.text: This part acts on 230 of 242 training patients (95%), and 99 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 55-year-old man with 0.6 mm of ST depression and a maximum heart rate of 154 beats per minute), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 20% to about 19% (on the training data only).
Through it, non-anginal chest pain and a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; the model has little data on this) each change the predicted risk only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_38.text: Through this part, a thallium result coded 4 raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 76% (2 patients; the model has little data on this; on the training data only).
It compares that code with all other thallium results taken together.

ann_39.text: Through this part, going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 96%, a flat ST segment raises it to about 77%, higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 12% to about 40%, and more ST depression (0 to 2.8 mm) from about 16% to about 38% (on the training data only).

Through it, being a woman lowers the predicted risk to about 1%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 8% and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute from about 27% to about 17%, while chest pain brought on by exercise raises it to about 32% (on the training data only).

Signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (about 24%) and an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG (2 patients, so the model has little data on this; about 25%) raise it only slightly through this part (on the training data only).

ann_40.text: Through this part, age changes a typical patient's predicted risk only slightly (on the training data only).
Going from 42 to 66 years moves it only slightly, from about 16% to about 18%, and not steadily in one direction (on the training data only).

ann_41.text: Through this part, higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 17% to about 25%, and an ST segment that does not slope up at peak exercise raises it from about 20% to about 28% (on the training data only).
Higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk more if the ST segment does not slope up (from about 72% to about 88%, against about 17% to about 25% with an upsloping ST segment).

ann_42.text: Through this part, the model clearly gives a typical patient a lower predicted risk with typical angina (about 1%), non-anginal chest pain (about 2%) or atypical angina (about 9%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 20%).
A downsloping ST segment raises it only slightly here (17 patients; the model has little data on this; on the training data only).

ann_43.text: Through this part, a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 40% (on the training data only).
A fixed defect lowers it to about 6% (15 patients) and a thallium result coded 4 raises it to about 89% (2 patients); the model has little data on this, and both hold on the training data only.

ann_44.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 1%), non-anginal chest pain (about 2%) or atypical angina (about 9%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 20%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 20% to about 96%, a flat ST segment raises it to about 83%, higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 12% to about 40%, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) from about 16% to about 38%, and a reversible thallium defect to about 40% (on the training data only).

Chest pain brought on by exercise raises it to about 32% and higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) from about 17% to about 25%, while being a woman lowers it to about 1%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 8%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute from about 27% to about 17% (on the training data only).

The model has little data on three categories: a thallium result coded 4 (2 patients; about 89%), a fixed defect on the thallium scan (15 patients; about 6%) and a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 28%), all on the training data only.

Signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG (about 24%), an ST-T wave abnormality (2 patients, so the model has little data on this; about 25%) and age (about 16% at 42 and 18% at 66 years) change it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_34.original: 1499 = relu(1.045 age_z - 0.478): an older-age hinge. It is zero below age_z=0.457 (about 59 years: train mean 54.8, SD 9.09) and rises linearly above it. It is read out to the logit with weight -0.423 (through identity_age), so for patients over ~59 it cancels and then reverses the direct +0.179 age slope (net -0.263 per SD). ann_35.original: 3392 = relu(0.587 + 1.332 trestbps_z + 0.907 slope:1_z): a resting-BP hinge whose threshold depends on upsloping ST (slope:1). Without upsloping ST it switches on above trestbps of about 136 mmHg; with upsloping ST, above about 111 mmHg (train mean 132.3, SD 18.2). Read out with weight -0.293, it damps the direct BP slope at high BP and gives upsloping ST a negative (protective) effect whenever the gate is open. ann_40.original: Age shape function: identity_age = 0.179 age_z - 0.423 age_gate(age_z) = 0.179 age_z - 0.423 relu(1.045 age_z - 0.478). This is an inverted-U in the logit: it rises with age to a peak near 59 years (+0.05), then falls (-0.09 at 65, -0.24 at 70, -0.44 at 77; -0.39 at 35). So the model treats middle-to-late-50s as the riskiest age and gives the oldest patients a lower risk than the direct slope alone would. This is an evolved non-monotone age effect, a small one.
